questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$*
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$

$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=6x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=6y(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].$*
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4t{e}^{6t} \\ -4{e}^{6t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1))\, \\ \,3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1))\,\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
